newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-MONEY FAILS TO BUY PREMIER LEAGUE SUCCESS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-MONEY FAILS TO BUY PREMIER LEAGUE SUCCESS.

text.p: Manchester United's title win and Middlesbrough's dramatic relegation suggest the premier league remains a meritocracy in which money cannot necessarily buy success.
When the English season kicked off in August it seemed hard cash was sure to triumph over hard work.

Newcastle had just paid a world record 15.0 million pounds ($24.4 million) for Alan Shearer, Chelsea had started to import half of Italy's serie A and Middlesbrough had forked out 11 million pounds ($17.9 million) to team up Fabrizio Ravanelli and Emerson with Juninho.
England was the place to play. Sterling was the currency to be paid in.

In the end though, glitzy Middlesbrough crashed out of the top flight, cash-strapped Leicester won the League Cup after struggling up from the first division the previous year and the championship went, once again, to a club where parsimony continues to rule.
Manchester United are, of course, among the very richest clubs in the world.
But they spent less on new players in the 1996 close season than any team in the premier league apart from Wimbledon, who also enjoyed a fine season and were unlucky to miss out on a place in Europe.

The revelation of United's season was Norwegian Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, who arrived at Old Trafford from Norwegian club Molde for a miserly 1.5 million pounds ($2.43) and finished the season as the club's top scorer with 18 league goals.

And David Beckham emerged as a world class talent in midfield -- further vindication of a youth team policy which has also produced Gary and Philip Neville, Paul Scholes and Nicky Butt, all of them now England squad members.
United once again faltered on the continent but the experience they gained from their progression to the semifinals of the European Cup will undoubtedly stand them in good stead there next season.

Contrast that with Middlesbrough, who face the almost certain break-up of their talented but exasperating side in the summer -- regardless of the outcome of next Saturday's F.A. Cup final in which they face Chelsea.
Middlesbrough may contest a points deduction which ultimately led to their downfall but they appear unlikely to succeed.
Barring a major upset in the courts, next season's visitors to the high-tech Riverside stadium will be the likes of Port Vale, Reading and Swindon rather than Liverpool, Arsenal and Newcastle.
Newcastle's late gallop into the runners-up spot and, consequently, a place alongside United in the European Cup, will make up in part for the disappointment of another season without a trophy.
The style in which Newcastle claimed second place owed as much to their previous manager Kevin Keegan as it did to current boss Kenny Dalglish.
A cavalier 5-0 defeat of relegated Nottingham Forest on Sunday ensured the team that Keegan built finished the campaign as the second most prolific side in the table behind United.
Dalglish has added backbone to Newcastle's attractive team and their late surge suggests they will again be in the title hunt next time around.
Liverpool, who, like United, spent modestly and wisely in the close season, will be disappointed with their fourth place after pressing United hard until the final weeks of the season.
Their erratic home form, two defeats at the hands of their arch-rivals from Manchester and a dreadful away performance in Paris in the Cup Winners' Cup wrecked a season which had promised so much.
Arsenal will be happier with their third place at the end of a campaign which began with one crisis after another.

The sacking of manager Bruce Rioch five days before the opening match, the controversial arrival of Frenchman Arsene Wenger in Rioch's wake and captain Tony Adams's admission to alcoholism all seem like dim and distant memories.

At the foot of the table, Forest paid a heavy price for a lack of fire-power up front and Sunderland fulfilled many pre-season predictions by returning to the first division after a single season in the big time.

Coventry and Southampton once again performed miracles to survive on shoe-string budgets and Leicester and Derby -- ninth and 12th respectively -- will be more than happy with their first season back in the top flight.
It was supposed to be the season in which the premier league effectively split in two, with a cluster of rich clubs sweeping all before them.
In the end though, 41 points separated top from bottom, 12 fewer than in 1995-96.
That can only be good for the English game -- what the premier league needs now is a team capable of breaking the Manchester United stranglehold.
